results.summary: This analog telephone hybrid converts two unidirectional signal paths into a single bidirectional line, using a transformer-based circuit. It is tested by connecting a wire between LINE1 and LINE2, then verifying that signals applied to IN1 appear at OUT2 and vice versa. External analog test equipment such as a function generator and oscilloscope is required for evaluation. Silicon measurements show operation up to about 3 kHz with 12–15 dB isolation, and the design requires band-limited input signals to maintain directionality.

This 8-bit hybrid adder combines a 4-bit Kogge-Stone adder with a 4-bit carry-lookahead adder to balance gate efficiency and latency. It takes two 8-bit operands on ui_in and uio_in and produces the sum on uo_out. Testing requires only applying 3.3V logic levels to the inputs and reading the outputs. The design is notable for being faster than an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder and more gate-efficient than an 8-bit carry-lookahead adder.

This design implements a forward pass for a simple artificial neural network with 4 input neurons, 8 hidden neurons, and 1 output neuron, and also computes the mean squared error loss. It accepts a 4-bit input on ui_in[3:0] and uses ui_in[7] to start the computation, with the result and state available on the output pins. External hardware consists of switches to set the input value and a button or switch to trigger the forward pass. The design is intended for inference and loss calculation, and can be simulated by modifying the test script.

This instrumented ring oscillator allows selection of the number of stages and initial state via input pins, and outputs 16 phases for observation. It is intended for studying the decay or persistence of high-frequency modes, not as a reliable clock source. Testing involves connecting a logic analyzer or oscilloscope to the outputs, configuring the stage count and seed, then enabling the oscillator and observing whether it stabilizes to the longest period or retains high-frequency modes. External hardware such as a logic analyzer or multi-channel oscilloscope is recommended for capturing the phase outputs.

This is a software-defined radio core for AM reception that uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC and performs digital bandpass filtering and envelope detection. It is configured via a SPI interface to set the demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs a PWM signal representing the demodulated audio. External hardware includes a comparator, resistor bias network, RC network, SPI microcontroller, and an RF amplifier. The design is notable for its compact 1x2 tile size, trading off selectivity compared to a previous larger implementation.

This design implements a linear feedback shift register with synaptic neuron-inspired behavior, where bit transitions generate excitatory or inhibitory signals that modify the feedback path. It accepts an 8-bit seed on the input pins and produces an 8-bit pseudo-random output sequence on uo_out. Testing involves providing a clock and reset, setting the seed, and observing the output sequence over multiple cycles. No external hardware is required, and the design allows customizable seed values to vary the output sequence.

This project implements a dynamic threshold leaky integrate-and-fire model that simulates a spiking biological neuron. The documentation is essentially placeholder text and does not describe how the model works or how to test it. The pin names suggest eight inputs and eight outputs, but their functions are not explained. No external hardware is mentioned, and the design cannot be evaluated from the available information.

This 8-bit carry-skip adder uses two 4-bit sections with skip logic to reduce carry propagation delay compared to a ripple-carry adder. It takes two 8-bit operands on ui_in and uio_in and outputs the registered sum on uo_out after each rising clock edge. Testing can be done by applying input values and verifying the output against expected sums, either manually or with a testbench. No external hardware is required.

This design multiplies two 2-bit 2x2 matrices, accepting matrix A on the standard input pins and matrix B on the bidirectional pins, and outputting the result matrix C on the standard output pins. Each matrix element is 2 bits, and the pin mapping is explicitly documented. Testing requires pulling pins high or low to set the input matrices and reading the output pins for the product. No external hardware is needed.

This project is a test harness for an OpenRAM SRAM macro (32x16) that communicates via UART, with separate address and data phases for read and write operations. It includes a DPU that can read, operate on, and write back data in the SRAM. Testing requires sending UART commands, ensuring the first command is sent only when uart_ready is high. Silicon tests confirmed random read/write functionality at 25 MHz and up to 75 MHz, with errors appearing at 100 MHz.
